extracted_by: hand, T-0290 — the Democrat read, August 1834
note: Vol. I No. 37, AND THE RICHEST ISSUE IN THE AUGUST RUN. The town news is NOT on page 3 this week: page 2 columns 5 and 6 carry the local editorial matter, and it holds the month's three biggest claims — the five men elected trustees of the town, the North Pier being pushed across the sand-bar by about a hundred hands under Lieut. Allen, and the town's own count of itself at 'over two thousand five hundred' people. Page 3 column 3 is the Tesseract fallback and is the CLEANEST text in the whole corpus so far, which is why the Marsh & Simons dissolution, the mechanic's lien on Lot 3 Block 111, Beaubien's administrator notice, the Briggs & Humphrey carriage shop on Randolph street and Botsford's factory at Lake and Dearborn are all readable almost without supply. Page 2 columns 5 and 6 are woven line by line as two sub-columns of one printed column, so each claim there names only its own lines and its bracketed supplies are read off the tails in the other column, line by line, with the lines named in the notes.

claims.notes: THE FIVE MEN WHO GOVERNED THIS TOWN IN THE YEAR BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, named in one sentence: John H. Kinzie, Gordon S. Hubbard, J. K. Boyer, Ebenezer Goodrich and John S. C. Hogan, elected trustees for one year on Monday 11 August 1834. Four of the five already stand in this reconstruction as merchants or as the postmaster; this is the claim that says they were also the board that passed the ordinances printed on page 4 of the same run — the South Water Street graduation (1834-07-30, claim c001 there) and the revenue ordinance are the acts of this body. THE PARAGRAPH IS CUT DOWN ITS RIGHT EDGE and its tails are in the NEXT segmenter column: 'rdon S. Hub-' (line 2400), 'oodrich and J.' (2402), 'ustees of thie' (2404) and 'at an election' (2406). Every bracketed supply above is read off those four lines and nothing else. THE FORENAME 'Gordon' AND THE SURNAME 'Goodrich' ARE SUPPLIED THAT WAY and are therefore readings, not certainties — but both men are documented in this town by other sources, and no other Hub- or G- name in the corpus fits the letters that survive.

claims.notes: THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL CLAIM IN THE AUGUST RUN, AND IT IS ABOUT THE GROUND ITSELF: in August 1834 the North Pier is being pushed out into the lake, across the sand-bar that lay opposite the river's mouth, by about a hundred hands under an army lieutenant — and MORE HANDS ARE STILL WANTED. What the town expected from it is stated in the same sentence: a channel protected from the north-east winds, of sufficient depth to admit vessels of the larger class INTO THE RIVER. The schooner Illinois had cut the bar in July 1834 and this is the work that kept it open. THE PARAGRAPH IS WOVEN LINE BY LINE with a recipe for glue and a note about a damaged steamboat, so `lines_of_claim` names only the fifteen lines that carry the harbor and five ambiguous single-word lines in the range ('Com-', 'ted.', 'Titer.', 'omplete.') are LEFT OUT rather than assigned by guess. EVERY BRACKETED SUPPLY IS READ OFF THE RIGHT-HAND TAILS IN SEGMENTER COLUMN 6 of the same page — 'work is now in ra-' (2273), 's it before present-' (2275), 'eue as at the pres-' (2277), 'fred bands are em-' (2279), 'I more are still wan-' (2281), 'it shall be exten.' (2283), 'pully extending in-' (2284), 'ying opposite the' (2287), 'the channel shall' (2289), 'th Enst winds, we' (2290), 'of sufficient depth' (2293), 'ger class into the' (2295), 'ery active and effi-' (2297), 'J. ALtes, much' (2299) — and the two halves agree line for line, which is what makes the reading a reconstruction rather than a guess. THE SUPERINTENDENT'S NAME reaches us as 'J. ALtes' in that tail; Lieut. James Allen of the U. S. Army commanded the Chicago harbor works in 1834, and the initial and the letter-shapes support it. The same officer is claimed on 1834-07-09 (claim c015 there) as '[uncertain: Lt. Allen]'; this is the second witness.

claims.notes: THE TOWN COUNTS ITSELF, IN PASSING, WHILE COMPLAINING ABOUT THE POST. 'A population of over two thousand five hundred' is the Democrat's own figure for Chicago in August 1834 — eleven months before the scene date, for which this project carries about 3,265 (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1) — and it is stated as an argument for a more frequent mail rather than as a census, which is worth knowing about it. THE SAME SENTENCE INVENTORIES THE TOWN as its editor saw it: a garrison of troops, important public works in progress (the harbor, claim c002), and an Indian Agency through which the Government was then negotiating the ratification of a treaty (claim c019). The join is what makes the number readable at all, and it is bracketed as a supply. THE OTHER TAILS used above are at 2315, 2318, 2320, 2322, 2325, 2327, 2329, 2337, 2339 and 2342 in column 6.

claims.notes: A MORTALITY FIGURE FOR THIS TOWN, PRINTED BY A MAN DEFENDING IT: twelve deaths in ten months, two or three of them children, one of old age and one of consumption, in a place of over two thousand people — offered against the reports 'frequently circulated that our town is unhealthy'. It is the editor's arithmetic and not a bill of mortality, and the claim records it as such. THE CHOLERA IS THE REASON THE SUBJECT IS LIVE: the 1832 epidemic had come to Fort Dearborn with Scott's troops, and this notice is tracking it back up the lakes — subsiding in the South, appearing in the eastern towns, raging at Quebec, and reported at Detroit with three cases. It had not reached Chicago in August 1834. TWO LINES OF THE QUOTE CARRY BOTH COLUMNS AT ONCE ('of the Des old age, and another of consu' at 2168, 'half mainder of different diseases,' at 2171) because the segmenter merged the two sub-columns on those rows; they are quoted verbatim, with the foreign words left standing, and unshuffled only in the normalized reading.

claims.notes: THE WHOLE SLATE, PRINTED WHOLE — which is what makes the cut printing of 1834-08-06 (claim c001 there) readable, and every forename bracketed in that claim is read off these lines. FOR THIS RECONSTRUCTION THE SHERIFF'S COLUMN IS THE INTERESTING ONE: Russel E. Heacock, this town's first resident lawyer, and George W. Snow, the surveyor and lumber dealer to whom the balloon frame is usually credited, both stood for county sheriff in 1834 — two men whose buildings and trades this project already carries, in a list of six candidates for one office. THE COLUMN IS WOVEN with a comic essay about hot weather, so the slate arrives one name per two lines and the office headings survive as 'For Lieut.', 'For', 'Senator to the', 'For County Co'. Names are minted here ONLY where the line carries the name whole; 'M. Jenk', 'William L.' and '[uncertain: K.] Brownson' are read in the normalized text and left out of the entity list.

Bates jr., whose auction store on the street to the drawbridge is claimed three times in this corpus.

claims.notes: RULING 3'S VETO, IN THE FORM THE RULING NAMES: a dissolution notice, signed by both partners, dated in this town. Marsh & Simons is dissolved on 6 August 1834 and therefore does NOT stand in the 1835 town — `contradicts` is set on this claim so the compiler computes it rather than an author asserting it. WHAT SURVIVES THE FIRM IS THE PLACE: Edward Simons goes on supplying the town at the Boston Market (claim c009), which is how a business that ends leaves a building behind. SILVESTER MARSH is the same man who later built the Mount Washington Cog Railway and made a fortune in Chicago packing; this is him at the very beginning, dissolving a market stall partnership. The column is the Tesseract fallback and is the cleanest text in the issue, so this claim needs almost no supply.

claims.notes: A NAMED CORNER, PRINTED IN THE CLEAN COLUMN: the tin, sheet iron and copper factory at the CORNER OF LAKE AND DEARBORN STREETS. That is a placement this reconstruction can put a building on, and the same corner is set again in the issue of 1834-08-27 at page 4 as 'CORNER OF DEARBOR[N] A[ND LAKE]' (line 4127), so it survives two printings. WHAT THE FACTORY TOOK IN PAYMENT is the other half of the claim and says as much about the town as the corner does: ginseng thoroughly dried, raccoon and deer skins, old pewter, copper and brass, and clean cotton and linen rags — a cash AND BARTER factory, in a town where cash was scarce. J. K. Botsford also advertises feathers, window sash, glass and whiskey two inches above (line 2785), from the same establishment.

claims.notes: A NAMED BUILDING IN USE ON A NAMED EVENING: the Chicago Temperance Society meets in the PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH at half-past seven on Thursday 14 August 1834. This project carries the First Presbyterian Church as a structure and the Baptist church as another; a meeting notice is the strongest kind of evidence for what a church building was actually used for. PHILO CARPENTER, the druggist of South Water Street (1834-07-02, claim c054 there), signs as secretary — the same man who had helped found the church. The claim also dates the Society itself, which this corpus had not previously placed.

claims.notes: THE 1833 TREATY OF CHICAGO, ITS RATIFICATION, AND A WARNING PRINTED IN THE TOWN'S OWN PAPER — dated at the Indian Agency in Chicago, 18 July 1834, and standing through August. It is read here for what it states and nothing more: the treaty of 26 September 1833 was ratified with conditions; until those conditions were assented to on the part of the Indians, persons presuming to settle on the ceded lands would be immediately removed. THE PROJECT'S STANDING CONSTRAINT APPLIES TO ANY USE MADE OF THIS (AGENTS.md): the final removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago falls in August 1835, inside the target year, and nothing in this reconstruction depicts Native presence without consultation. The claim is filed because the Indian Agency is a documented institution of this town with a named agent, and because the notice fixes what the agency was doing in the month it was printed. THE BETTER PRINTING IS 1834-08-20, page 3 column 5, lines 3379-3392, which carries 'THE Chicago Treaty of the 26th' and 'of Clark' whole; the supplies above are read off it and are bracketed.

claims.notes: ONE IMPRESSION OF THE STANDING LAKE STREET LAND-AGENCY CARD. The Democrat sets this advertisement, word for word the same, in every issue from 1834-05-14 to 1834-10-01 — twenty consecutive weeks, eighteen of which set the line ‘purchased and Sold, or by commi[s]sion’ recognisably (T-1051). The card is identified by its copy and not by its display line: the same trade (‘House and Land Agent’), the same offer of building lots in the town and the School Section, the same houses to let, and the same office on Lake street opposite Dr. Temple's. The display line is lost — line 2953 closes P. Pruyne & Co.'s notice immediately above. THE PROPRIETOR'S NAME IS NOT READ HERE and none is supplied into the quote: the record's ‘W. G. Blanchard’ stands on T-0408's reading of the two impressions whose columns are NOT Tesseract fallbacks (1834-07-16 line 5527, 1834-09-17 line 3292) and on identity.json's declared firm merge, not on this impression. THE ADDRESS LINE IS PRESENT AND UNREADABLE: line 2957 sets 'Take st mouse r. Tampingure at the office:', which is the card's 'Lake st. opposite Dr. Temple's. Enquire at the Office on' collapsed into one line and mangled past the point where either the street or the anchor can be read off it. It is quoted where it stands and this printing is recorded as SILENT about placement — not given the address its neighbours print — which is the difference between reading a line and recognising a card. 2959 sets 'school section.' after 'Houses to Let', out of the card's order.
